data.explanation:
The verb **"to be"** is one of the first verbs you need in English. You use it to say who someone is, what something is, or how someone feels.

The form changes with the subject. Use **"am"** with **"I"**, **"is"** with **"he"**, **"she"**, and **"it"**, and **"are"** with **"you"**, **"we"**, and **"they"**.

data.explanation:
Subject pronouns are small words that take the place of a name. You use them at the start of a sentence, before the verb. They help you talk about people and things without saying the name again.

The subject pronouns are **"I"**, **"you"**, **"he"**, **"she"**, **"it"**, **"we"**, and **"they"**. Use **"he"** for a man, **"she"** for a woman, and **"it"** for a thing or an animal. **"We"** means you and other people. **"They"** means more than one person or thing.
"I am busy."
"She is a doctor."
"They live near here."

Always write **"I"** with a big letter. Don't use **"me"** at the start of a sentence. Say "I am fine", not "Me am fine".

data.explanation:
Object pronouns are the small words you use after a verb or after words like **"to"**, **"for"**, and **"with"**. They show who or what gets the action.

The object pronouns are **"me"**, **"you"**, **"him"**, **"her"**, **"it"**, **"us"**, and **"them"**. Most of them are different from the subject form. **"I"** becomes **"me"**, **"he"** becomes **"him"**, **"she"** becomes **"her"**, **"we"** becomes **"us"**, and **"they"** becomes **"them"**. Only **"you"** and **"it"** stay the same.
"Can you help me?"
"I like him."
"Sit next to her."

Don't say "Give it to I". It's wrong. After **"to"**, you need the object form.

data.explanation:
Possessive adjectives show that something belongs to someone. They always go right before a noun. You can't use them alone.

The words are **"my"**, **"your"**, **"his"**, **"her"**, **"its"**, **"our"**, and **"their"**. Use **"his"** for a man, **"her"** for a woman, and **"its"** for a thing or an animal. **"Our"** is for **"we"**, and **"their"** is for **"they"**.
"This is my phone."

Don't say "the my car". Just say "my car". The form is the same for one thing and for many things. Be careful: **"its"** means belonging to it, but **"it's"** means **"it is"**. These are two different words.
"My bags are heavy."

**"A"** and **"an"** mean one thing, but not a special one. You use them when you talk about something for the first time, or when it doesn't matter which one.

data.explanation:
Use **"the"** when you and the other person both know which thing you mean. It can be because you talked about it before, or because there is only one in the place.

A common pattern is to use **"a"** or **"an"** the first time, and **"the"** the second time.
"I saw a dog. The dog was friendly."

You also use **"the"** when there is only one of something in the room or place. Everyone knows which one.
"Close the door."
"Where is the station?"

Don't use **"the"** with most names of people, cities, or countries. Say "Maria is here", not "The Maria is here". For general ideas, don't use **"the"**. Say "I like pizza", not "I like the pizza".

"Two men are waiting."

data.explanation:
Possessive pronouns are words that show who owns something. The big difference from **"my"** or **"your"** is that they stand alone. No noun comes after them.

The words are **"mine"**, **"yours"**, **"his"**, **"hers"**, **"ours"**, and **"theirs"**. You use them when you don't want to say the noun again.

data.explanation:
To make a negative or a question in the present simple, you need a helper verb. English uses **"do"** and **"does"** for this. They don't have their own meaning here. They just help the sentence.

Use **"do"** with **"I"**, **"you"**, **"we"**, and **"they"**. Use **"does"** with **"he"**, **"she"**, and **"it"**. For negatives, add **"not"** after the helper. "I don't eat breakfast."

The main question words are **"who"**, **"what"**, **"where"**, **"when"**, **"why"**, and **"how"**. "How are you?"

data.explanation:
Place prepositions are small words that tell you where something is. You need them to describe a room or to find things.

The most useful ones are **"in"**, **"on"**, **"under"**, **"next to"**, **"behind"**, **"in front of"**, and **"between"**. Use **"in"** for inside something. Use **"on"** for on top of a surface. Use **"under"** for below something.

English uses three small words to talk about time: **"in"**, **"on"**, and **"at"**. Each one has its own job.

Numbers and time come up every day. You need them for shopping, travel, and meetings. A few fixed patterns will help you a lot.

For age, use the verb **"be"**, not **"have"**. Say "She is 12 years old". Don't say "She has 12 years". For dates, use **"on"**. For clock times, use **"at"**.

data.summary: Use the past simple to talk about finished actions in the past with regular verbs.

data.explanation:
The **"past simple"** is the tense you use for finished actions. If it happened yesterday, last week, or at any clear point in the past, use the **"past simple"**. The action is over and done.

For regular verbs, add **"-ed"** to make the past form. Watch becomes **"watched"**, clean becomes **"cleaned"**, play becomes **"played"**. A few verbs double the final consonant: stop becomes **"stopped"**, plan becomes **"planned"**.
"I walked to the station this morning."

Be careful with verbs ending in **"-e"** -- you just add **"-d"**: like becomes **"liked"**, use becomes **"used"**. And with verbs ending in consonant + **"-y"**, change the **"-y"** to **"-ied"**: study becomes **"studied"**.
"They studied together before the exam."
Always use a past time word or context with this tense. "I go yesterday" is wrong -- use "I went yesterday".

data.summary: Use common irregular past forms to talk about finished past events.

Irregular verbs don't follow the **"-ed"** rule. Each one has its own past form that you need to learn. This sounds hard, but the most common English verbs are irregular -- so you'll meet them again and again.

Some key pairs to know: **"go"** becomes **"went"**, **"see"** becomes **"saw"**, **"have"** becomes **"had"**, **"eat"** becomes **"ate"**, **"come"** becomes **"came"**, **"take"** becomes **"took"**. The past form is the same for every subject -- no extra endings.

data.explanation:
**"Quantifiers"** tell you how much or how many. The word you choose depends on the type of noun -- **"countable"** (things you can count) or **"uncountable"** (things treated as a mass or substance).

**"Many"** and **"a few"** go with countable plurals. **"Much"** and **"a little"** go with uncountable nouns. **"A lot of"** works with both. In positive sentences, **"many"** and **"much"** can sound formal -- **"a lot of"** is more natural in everyday speech.
"There aren't many buses after ten."

**"A few"** and **"a little"** have a positive feeling -- they mean "some". **"Few"** and **"little"** without **"a"** have a negative feeling -- they mean "not enough".
"I have a few friends in this city." (some, that's good) vs. "I have few friends here." (not many, that's a problem)

data.title: Countable and Uncountable Nouns
data.summary: Know which nouns can be counted and which are treated as amounts or substances.

examples.en: I need a glass and a plate.

data.explanation:
Some nouns can be counted individually -- one chair, two chairs. These are **"countable nouns"**. Other nouns refer to substances, ideas, or things treated as a mass -- water, advice, furniture. These are **"uncountable nouns"**.

The difference matters because it changes how you use articles, quantifiers, and verb agreement. Countable nouns can take **"a/an"** and a plural form. Uncountable nouns don't.
"I need a chair and two plates." (countable)
"We bought some bread and a bottle of water." (uncountable)

Some nouns surprise people. **"Advice"**, **"information"**, **"news"**, **"furniture"**, and **"luggage"** are all uncountable in English, even though they might be countable in other languages. Use **"some"** or a partitive phrase instead.
"Can I give you some advice?" not "Can I give you an advice?"
To talk about a unit of an uncountable noun, use a container or measure word: a piece of advice, a glass of water, a loaf of bread.

data.explanation:
Not all questions work the same way. Some ask about the subject -- the person or thing doing the action. Others ask about the object -- the person or thing the action happens to. The word order is different for each.

When you ask about the **"object"**, you use **"do/does/did"** and the word order changes: Who did you call? What did she eat? When you ask about the **"subject"**, no **"did"** is needed and the word order stays normal: Who called you? What happened?

A good test: if the question word is the subject (doing the action), skip **"did"**. If the question word is the object (receiving the action), add **"did"**.
"What made that noise?" (subject -- something made the noise)
"What did you hear?" (object -- you heard something)

data.title: Must, Mustn't, and Have To
data.summary: Use these forms to express obligation, necessity, and prohibition.

examples.en: You must show your ticket at the door.
I have to finish this report today.
Passengers mustn't smoke here.
She has to wear glasses for reading.

data.explanation:
**"Must"**, **"mustn't"**, and **"have to"** all deal with rules and obligations -- but they don't mean the same thing, and mixing them up causes real problems.

**"Must"** usually comes from the speaker -- it's personal or internal. **"Have to"** usually comes from an outside rule or situation. Both mean something is necessary, but the source is different.
"You must wear a badge." (rule I'm telling you)
"I have to leave at six -- my train is at six-fifteen." (external situation)

The key contrast is between **"mustn't"** and **"don't have to"**. These are completely different.
**"Mustn't"** = it is forbidden, don't do it: "You mustn't smoke in here."
**"Don't have to"** = it is not necessary, but you can if you want: "You don't have to come -- it's optional."
Saying "You mustn't do it if you don't want to" when you mean it's optional is a serious error. Use **"don't have to"** for things that are not required.

**"Could"** and **"would"** make you sound more polite and flexible. At this level, focus on the most common uses you'll need in everyday conversation.

**"Because"** and **"so"** both connect two ideas, but they do opposite jobs. **"Because"** introduces the reason. **"So"** introduces the result. Mixing them up changes the meaning completely.

data.explanation:
**"Reflexive pronouns"** are used when the subject and the object of the verb are the same person or thing. The action comes back to the same person doing it.

The forms are: I -> **"myself"**, you -> **"yourself"**, he -> **"himself"**, she -> **"herself"**, it -> **"itself"**, we -> **"ourselves"**, you (plural) -> **"yourselves"**, they -> **"themselves"**. Match the reflexive pronoun to the subject.
"He cut himself while he was cooking."
"She taught herself some basic Spanish."

You can also use reflexive pronouns for emphasis -- to say that someone did something without any help.
"I made this cake myself." (no one helped me)
"They painted the whole house themselves."
Don't use a reflexive pronoun when a normal object pronoun works: "She looked at herself in the mirror" is correct (same person), but "She helped him" -- not "herself" -- when helping a different person.

data.explanation:
The **present perfect** links your past experiences to who you are right now. You use it when you want to talk about things you have done at some point in your life, without saying exactly when they happened.

Form it with **"have"** or **"has"** + **past participle**. Common signals are **"ever"**, **"never"**, and **"before"**.

Knowing each tense alone is not enough at B1. You need to choose between them. The core distinction: use the **past simple** for a clearly finished time, and the **present perfect** when no finished time is mentioned or the period is still open.

Time words are your clearest guide. Finished-time words -- **"yesterday"**, **"last week"**, **"in 2019"**, **"when I was young"** -- go with the **past simple**. "I've seen that film." (no time given -- just a life experience)

data.explanation:
Five small words appear constantly with the **present perfect**, and each one carries a specific job. Getting them right is one of the clearest signs of solid B1 control.

**"For"** goes with a length of time. **"Since"** goes with a starting point.
"I've worked here for three years." (a duration)
"She's lived there since 2020." (a point when it started)
**"Yet"** appears in negatives and questions for something expected: "I haven't finished yet. Have you called her yet?" **"Already"** shows something happened sooner than expected: "He's already left." **"Just"** means very recently: "I've just sent it."

Position matters. **"Already"** and **"just"** usually sit before the past participle. **"Yet"** usually comes at the end of the sentence. Confusing "for" and "since" is the most common mistake at this level -- "I've lived here since three years" is wrong; it should be "for three years".

The **first conditional** is for real, possible future situations. You see the condition as genuinely likely -- not just imagined. You are saying: if this happens, that will follow.

The pattern is **"if"** + **present simple**, then **"will"** + **base verb**. The if-clause uses the present simple even though the meaning is future -- this is one of the most common learner errors.

The **second conditional** is for situations that are not real -- things you are imagining, unlikely scenarios, or advice about hypothetical choices. You are not expecting these situations to happen.

data.explanation:
**Reported speech** lets you tell someone what another person said, without repeating their exact words. When you do this, the tense in the reported part usually shifts back one step. This is called **backshift**.

The shift follows a clear pattern: **present simple** becomes **past simple**, **"will"** becomes **"would"**, and **present continuous** becomes **past continuous**.
Direct: "I'm tired." Reported: She said she was tired.
Direct: "I'll be late." Reported: He said he'd be late.

**"Said"** and **"told"** are both common reporting verbs, but they work differently. "Said" does not need an object: "She said she was ready." "Told" does: "She told me she was ready." Mixing them up is one of the most frequent mistakes at this level. Also notice that pronouns may need to change -- "I" might become "she" or "he" depending on who is speaking.

The **passive voice** shifts the focus from who does something to what happens. You use it when the person doing the action is unknown, obvious, or not relevant -- what matters is the thing affected.

examples.en: You've been working all day. You must be tired.

**Modal verbs** do not just express ability or obligation -- at B1 they become tools for making logical conclusions. You use **"must"**, **"might"**, and **"can't"** to interpret a situation and say what you think is true, possible, or impossible.

data.summary: Compare these forms to talk about obligation and necessity more precisely.

examples.en: I have to catch the last train home.

data.explanation:
**"Have to"**, **"must"**, and **"need to"** all express obligation or necessity, but they feel different in use. At B1, the real skill is choosing between them based on tone and source of the obligation.

**"Have to"** is for external rules or practical requirements. **"Must"** is stronger and more personal, or more formal -- often used in written rules and strong personal recommendations. **"Need to"** is neutral and practical.
"We have to wear ID badges at work." (a company rule -- external)
"You must try this -- it's incredible." (personal, strong recommendation)
"I need to call the bank before it closes." (practical necessity)

The biggest trap is the difference between **"mustn't"** and **"don't have to"**. "Mustn't" means it is prohibited. "Don't have to" means it is not necessary -- you have a choice. data.explanation:
A **defining relative clause** gives essential information about a noun. It tells you exactly which person or thing you mean. Without the clause, the sentence would be too vague or incomplete.

The three main pronouns are **"who"** (for people), **"which"** (for things), and **"that"** (can replace either in most everyday contexts). The clause follows directly after the noun it describes, with no comma.
"The woman who helped me was very kind." (which woman? -- the clause defines her)

Two common mistakes: using **"which"** for people ("the man which called") -- use "who" instead. And repeating the subject inside the clause: "the man who he works here" is wrong -- it should be "the man who works here". data.explanation:
**Phrasal verbs** are verb + particle combinations that appear constantly in everyday English. The particle -- usually a short word like **"up"**, **"out"**, **"on"**, or **"off"** -- combines with the verb to create a meaning that often is not obvious from the individual words.

The best way to learn them is in context, as whole phrases, not by trying to guess meaning from the parts.
"I wake up at 7, but I don't get up until 7:30." (wake up = stop sleeping; get up = leave the bed)
"Can you turn on the heater? And turn off the light when you leave." (opposite actions for devices)
"I've been looking for my keys for an hour." (look for = search for)

Do not translate phrasal verbs word-for-word from your own language -- that usually gives the wrong meaning. Watch out for opposite pairs: "turn on / turn off", "put on / take off". Learning them in pairs helps you remember both at once. More structure and a larger set come at B2.

data.explanation:
**"So"**, **"such"**, **"too"**, and **"enough"** all describe degree, but each one works in a different slot. Getting the pattern right makes a real difference to how natural your English sounds.

**"So"** goes before an **adjective or adverb**: "so tired", "so quickly". **"Such"** goes before a **noun phrase**: "such a long day", "such great food". If there is a noun, use "such". If there is only an adjective, use "so".
"It was so cold that we left early." (adjective only -- use "so")
"It was such a cold night that we left early." (adjective + noun -- use "such")
**"Too"** means more than acceptable: "This bag is too heavy to carry." **"Enough"** means sufficient. After an adjective: "She's tall enough." Before a noun: "We don't have enough chairs."

Do not use **"too"** where you mean "very" -- "too" usually signals a problem or impossibility, while "very" does not. Watch the position of "enough": it goes after the adjective but before the noun.

"The test wasn't as hard as I expected." (less difficulty than expected)
"He doesn't drive as carefully as his father." (with an adverb)

Two frequent mistakes: using the comparative form inside the pattern ("as faster as" is wrong -- use "as fast as"), and using **"than"** instead of the second **"as"** ("she isn't as tall than her sister" is wrong). **"Used to"** also carries an implied contrast with now -- "I used to play chess" usually means you do not anymore. **"Would"** does not carry that contrast as clearly. data.explanation:
By B1 you know several future forms. The real challenge is choosing between them. **"Will"**, **"be going to"**, and the **present continuous** all talk about the future -- but they signal different things.

**"Will"** is for instant decisions, offers, promises, and general predictions -- things decided in the moment. **"Be going to"** is for prior intentions and predictions based on visible evidence. The **present continuous** is best for fixed personal arrangements, especially when there is a specific time, place, or other person involved.
"The phone's ringing -- I'll get it." (instant decision)
"I'm going to start running in the mornings." (intention decided before now)
"I'm meeting Lea at 6." (already arranged, specific time and person)

Do not use **"will"** for everything. If the plan was already made, "going to" or the present continuous is more natural. If it is a fixed appointment with another person, the present continuous usually sounds best. "Look at those clouds -- it's going to rain" works because you have visible evidence right now.

data.explanation:
At B1, you need to use **subject questions** and **object questions** automatically. The key is asking: what information is missing -- the person or thing that did the action, or the person or thing that received it?

If you are asking about the **subject** -- who or what did the action -- the question word fills that role directly. No helper verb needed.
"Who called?" (who = subject; no "did")
"What happened?" (what = subject; no "did")
If you are asking about the **object** -- who or what received the action -- you need a helper verb.
"Who did you call?" (you = subject; "who" = object)
"What did she buy?" (she = subject; "what" = object)

The most common mistake is adding **"did"** to subject questions: "Who did arrive first?" is wrong -- just "Who arrived first?" The opposite error is also frequent: "What she bought?" is missing "did" -- it should be "What did she buy?"

data.explanation:
"Very" is useful, but it gets repetitive. At B1, you start using **"quite"**, **"rather"**, and **"fairly"** to give your descriptions more texture and precision. These are degree adverbs -- they all modify the strength of an adjective or adverb.

**"Fairly"** suggests a moderate, measured degree. **"Quite"** is similar but can be stronger depending on context and stress. **"Rather"** often adds a sense of surprise, stronger feeling, or something unexpected -- it has a slightly formal, often British tone.
"The film was fairly good." (positive, but not impressive -- measured)
"She's quite talented." (noticeably so -- stronger than "fairly")
"That was rather a strange thing to say." (unexpected or surprising)

All three go directly before the adjective or adverb they modify. Do not stack them with "very" -- "quite very long" does not work. And do not confuse them with **"too"** -- "too" signals a problem or excess, while "quite", "rather", and "fairly" are neutral or positive in degree.

data.title: Time Clauses (when, while, as soon as, until, before, after)
data.summary: Use time clauses to connect actions in sequence and show when one event happens in relation to another.

examples.en: Call me when you leave the office.

examples.en: I read the emails while I was waiting for the bus.

data.explanation:
**Time clauses** connect two events and show how they relate in time. Words like **"when"**, **"while"**, **"as soon as"**, **"until"**, **"before"**, and **"after"** each signal a different kind of time relationship.

**"When"** links a point in time to another event. **"While"** shows two things happening at the same time. **"As soon as"** means immediately after. **"Until"** gives an endpoint. **"Before"** and **"after"** show order.
"Call me when you leave." (at the point of leaving)
"She was reading while I was cooking." (simultaneous actions)
"As soon as he arrives, we'll start." (immediate sequence)

One of the most important rules: in future contexts, the time clause uses the **present simple**, not "will".
"I'll call you when I arrive." -- not "when I will arrive."
The main clause can use "will", but the time clause stays in the present simple. This trips up almost every B1 learner. Also, use **"while"** for two simultaneous actions, not "when" -- "When I was cooking, she arrived" works for two separate events, but "While I was cooking, she was reading" is more natural for two things at the same time.

data.explanation:
The **present perfect continuous** focuses on duration or ongoing activity that connects the past to the present. The key question it answers is "how long" -- not whether something happened, but how long it has been happening.

Form it with **have/has been** + verb-ing.
"I've been waiting for an hour."
"She's been working on that report since this morning." It also fits recent actions that just stopped but left a visible result: "You've been crying -- what happened?"

Compare with the **present perfect simple**, which highlights completion or a result, not duration.
"I've read that book." (completed)
"I've been reading that book all week." (ongoing effort) Both can be correct, but simple = result; continuous = duration. Also, **stative verbs** like know, like, and belong do not normally appear in continuous forms -- use the simple instead.

data.title: Past Perfect Continuous
data.summary: Use the past perfect continuous to show an ongoing earlier-past activity before another past point.

examples.en: We had been walking for hours before we found the village.

data.explanation:
The **past perfect continuous** looks back from a past moment and shows how long something had been happening before another event occurred. It is the tense for past-in-the-past duration, not just past-in-the-past completion.

Form it with **had been** + verb-ing.
"We had been waiting for an hour when the bus finally arrived."
"He was exhausted because he'd been driving all night." The ongoing activity explains or sets up the later past event.

Compare with the **past perfect simple**.
"She had called them." (completed act)
"She had been calling them all morning." (repeated effort over time) Use the continuous when duration is the point of the sentence. There also needs to be a past reference point -- a moment or event you're looking back from. Without it, the tense loses its purpose.

data.explanation:
The **third conditional** describes unreal past situations and their imagined results. You are not reporting what happened -- you are saying what would have happened if things had gone differently.

The pattern is: **if + past perfect**, **would have + past participle**.
"If we had left earlier, we would have caught the train."
"If she had checked the map, she wouldn't have got lost." Both halves are imagined. This structure works naturally for regret, criticism, and reflection on missed chances.

Two common errors: putting **would have** in the if-clause ("If I would have known" is wrong -- use the past perfect there), and using the past simple instead of the past perfect in the if-clause, which weakens or shifts the meaning. The if-clause and result clause can be swapped: "We would have saved money if we'd booked earlier." The meaning stays the same.

data.explanation:
**Mixed conditionals** link two different time frames in one sentence. The most common pattern takes an unreal past condition and connects it to a present result: the past is imagined differently, and the consequence plays out now.

The practical test: ask what time each clause belongs to. If the condition is past and the result is present, use the first pattern. If the condition is present and the result is past, use the second. The mistake most learners make is defaulting to a standard second or third conditional when the time split is actually across two different frames.

data.explanation:
**Wish** and **if only** both express that reality is not what you want it to be. The verb form after wish does not show past time -- it shows unreality. For present situations, the verb shifts back one tense.

"I wish I had more time." (present reality: I don't have enough time)
"If only she knew how much this matters." For past regrets, the pattern shifts to **wish + past perfect**.
"I wish I'd taken that course."
"If only I'd called him earlier." Same grammar as wish, but if only carries stronger emotion.

**If only** and **wish** are grammatically identical. The difference is tone -- if only tends to feel more intense or dramatic. **Modal perfect** forms let you reason about what probably, possibly, or impossibly happened in the past. Instead of stating facts, you are drawing conclusions from evidence.

data.title: Modal Perfect: Should Have, Could Have, Would Have
data.summary: Use modal perfect forms for regret, criticism, missed possibility, and unreal past results.

examples.en: You should have told me you were running late.

data.explanation:
**Modal perfect** forms evaluate the past -- they say something about what the right action was, what was possible, or what would have happened under different conditions.

**Should have** expresses criticism or regret: the action was expected or correct, but it did not happen.
"You should have called me." (you didn't, and that was wrong)
**Could have** points to a missed possibility.
"We could have taken a taxi, but we walked."
**Would have** signals an unreal result that depended on a condition.
"I would have helped if I'd known."

These come up constantly in discussions about mistakes, decisions, and imagined alternatives. Do not mix them up with **must have** or **can't have**, which are for logical deduction, not evaluation. And remember the pattern: modal + **have** + past participle, not base verb.
"You should have called" -- not "should have call."

By B2, the passive needs to work across multiple tenses, not just the present simple. You need forms like **is being repaired**, **was being cleaned**, **has been completed**, and **had been cancelled** to describe when and how things happen to people or objects.

The structure stays consistent: **be** in the required tense + **past participle**. The tense is carried entirely by the auxiliary verbs; the main verb always stays as a past participle.

The **causative** structure describes arranging for someone else to do something on your behalf. You are not doing the task -- you are organising it or having it done.

The pattern is: **have/get + object + past participle**.

Reporting questions is more complex than reporting statements because the word order changes. In direct speech, questions use inverted order: "Where do you live?" In reported speech, the inversion disappears and the clause becomes statement-like.

For **yes/no questions**, use **if** or **whether** to introduce the reported clause.
"She asked if I was free."
For **wh- questions**, keep the question word, but follow it with subject + verb.
"What did they order?" becomes "They asked what we had ordered." Backshift usually applies when the reporting verb is past, following the same rules as reported statements.

Two consistent errors: keeping the auxiliary inversion from the original question ("She asked where did I live" is wrong -- drop the inversion), and forgetting **if/whether** in yes/no reports. Both produce sentences that are either grammatically off or change the intended meaning.

At B2, **say** and **tell** are not precise enough. A wider set of reporting verbs lets you show exactly what kind of speech act took place -- admitting, denying, suggesting, warning, promising, accusing.

data.summary: Use non-defining relative clauses to add extra, non-essential information about a person or thing.

examples.en: Our car, which we bought second-hand, has been very reliable.

data.explanation:
**Non-defining relative clauses** add extra information about a noun that is already identified. Remove the clause and the sentence still makes complete sense -- the clause adds a detail, not a definition.

"My uncle, who lives in Ankara, is visiting us." The commas mark it as non-defining: we already know which uncle.
Use **who** for people, **which** for things, **whose** for possession.
"The hotel, which opened last year, is already fully booked."
"Sara, whose brother is a pilot, travels often."

Contrast this with a **defining relative clause**, where the clause is essential to identify the noun -- no commas there, and **that** is often acceptable.
"The student who sits near the window" -- without the clause, you do not know which student. The most common errors in non-defining clauses: forgetting the commas (which changes the clause type and its meaning) and using **that** where **which** or **who** is required.

data.explanation:
**Reduced relative clauses** shorten a full relative clause when the meaning stays clear without the relative pronoun and auxiliary.

These reductions are common in formal writing, signs, notices, and concise description -- contexts where tighter sentences are preferred. data.title: Linking Words of Result and Purpose
data.summary: Use varied structures to express purpose and consequence more precisely.

data.explanation:
**Result** and **purpose** are often expressed loosely with just **because** or **so**. At B2, more precise linkers let you signal the relationship clearly and at the right register.

**So that** introduces purpose and is followed by a clause.
"I left early so that I could catch the train."
**In order to** is followed by the base verb and sounds slightly more formal.
"We met in order to review the draft."
**Therefore** and **consequently** signal result and are common in formal writing and speech.
"The data were incomplete; therefore, we postponed the decision." They typically follow a semicolon or open a new sentence.

Purpose linkers answer "why was it done?"; result linkers show what followed. The most common mistake is using **so that** with an infinitive instead of a clause -- "I came early so that catch the train" does not work. data.explanation:
By B2, articles depend less on simple rules and more on conventions, meaning, and context. Some of the trickiest areas are geography, institutional nouns, and fixed expressions.

**Geography**: most country names take no article -- "We visited France." But some names do take **the** -- "We crossed through the Netherlands." Mountain ranges, rivers, and seas also take **the** -- "the Alps", "the Nile." These patterns need to be noticed and stored as you encounter them.
**Institutional nouns** shift meaning depending on the article.
"Go to school" = attend as a student. "Go to the school" = visit the building. The same logic applies to hospital, prison, university, and church in British English.

**Fixed expressions** often take no article at all: "at home", "in hospital", "by car", "on foot." Overusing **the** with place names, and missing the shift with institutional nouns, are the most common problems at this level.

data.summary: Choose the right determiner to talk about individuals, total groups, and complete units.

data.explanation:
**Each**, **every**, **all**, and **whole** all relate to groups or totality, but they work differently and cannot be swapped freely.

**Each** treats members separately, one by one: "Each student received a different task."
**Every** refers to all members of a group in a general or rule-like way: "Every applicant must sign the form." Both **each** and **every** take a singular noun and singular verb.
**All** refers to the total group taken together, usually with a plural noun and verb: "All the lights were on."
**Whole** refers to one complete, undivided unit with a singular noun: "She spent the whole afternoon on it."

Common errors: mixing **whole** and **all** ("the all day" is wrong -- say "all day" or "the whole day"), and using **each** with a plural noun in the wrong structure. Choosing between **each** and **every** often comes down to whether you want to stress individual members or a general rule.

When **negative or limiting adverbs** like **never**, **rarely**, or **seldom** are placed at the front of a sentence for emphasis, the auxiliary verb moves before the subject. This is called **inversion**, and it gives the sentence a formal or dramatic quality.

Ordinary order: "I have never seen such chaos."
With inversion: "Never have I seen such chaos."
"Rarely do we get results like this."
"Seldom has the team performed so well." The fronted adverb signals the inversion -- the auxiliary follows immediately, then the subject.

At B2, the goal is to recognise the pattern and use it confidently with a small set of common adverbs: **never**, **rarely**, **seldom**, **hardly ever**, **not only**. data.summary: Use participle clauses to make sentences shorter and show time, reason, or result more compactly.

examples.en: Walking through the park, I noticed the trees had changed colour.

data.explanation:
**Participle clauses** let you combine two ideas into one sentence more efficiently, replacing a full subordinate clause with a shorter form.

"As I was walking home, I called my sister." becomes "Walking home, I called my sister." Both share the same subject, so the reduction works cleanly.
**-ing clauses** are used for active meaning: "Feeling exhausted, she went straight to bed."
**Past participle clauses** are used for passive meaning: "Surprised by the news, he sat down in silence." Both can show time, reason, result, or an accompanying action.

These clauses are especially common in written English and formal speech. The main trap is a **dangling participle** -- using a participle clause when the subject of the clause differs from the subject of the main clause.
"Walking to the station, the rain started." This is wrong -- the rain was not walking. Always check that the participle's implied subject matches the main clause's subject.

data.explanation:
By B2, knowing what phrasal verbs mean is not enough -- you also need to know how they behave structurally. The key distinction is **separable** versus **inseparable**.

**Separable** phrasal verbs allow the object to go between the verb and particle, especially when the object is a pronoun.
"Turn off the music" or "Turn the music off" -- both work with a noun.
But with a pronoun, only the middle position is correct: "Turn it off." -- never "Turn off it."
**Inseparable** phrasal verbs cannot be split at all.
"She looks after her grandmother." -- you cannot say "She looks her grandmother after."
Common inseparable verbs: run into, come across, deal with, get over.

At B2, it is also worth expanding your active range: carry on, set up, work out, break down, give away, take over, put off, bring up. Learn each one with its separability at the same time as its meaning -- not as an afterthought.

data.summary: Use inversion after fronted negative or limiting expressions for formal emphasis and dramatic style.

examples.en: Hardly had I closed my laptop when the fire alarm started.

data.explanation:
**Inversion after negative adverbs** is one of the clearest markers of advanced formal English. When a negative or limiting expression is fronted, the auxiliary shifts before the subject - the word order flips. At C1 level, this pattern should feel like a deliberate stylistic choice, not a grammar exercise.

The pattern: **fronted trigger + auxiliary + subject + main verb**. Simple tenses that lack an auxiliary borrow **do/does/did**.
"Hardly had I sat down when the alarm went off."
"Not until the final page did the title make sense."
"On no account should this file be shared externally."

The register is formal - journalism, speeches, legal writing, literary prose. The most common error is fronting the trigger but keeping normal word order: "Not until midnight we got home" - the inversion is what makes the structure work. In casual conversation, these patterns sound theatrical, so save them for writing or prepared speech.

data.explanation:
**It-clefts** let you isolate one element of a sentence and put the spotlight squarely on it. The facts stay the same - only where the reader's attention goes changes. At C1 level, using clefts well is a sign of discourse control, not just grammar knowledge.

The pattern: **It + be + focused element + that/who + clause**. Use **who** for people, **that** for most other elements. The tense of **be** tracks your time reference.
"It was Maya who spotted the error, not the system."
"It is the deadline that worries me, not the workload."
"It was on Tuesday that they finally confirmed it."

Two errors are common: dropping the clause after the focus ("It was James sent the file" needs **who sent the file**), and using **what** instead of **that** inside an it-cleft. The contrastive use is one of the most natural homes for this structure - "It wasn't the delay that upset him; it was the silence" lands with real force.

data.summary: Use what-clefts and all-clefts to focus on actions, needs, or key information in a sentence.

data.explanation:
**What-clefts** and **all-clefts** put a different kind of information at the centre of a sentence. Rather than spotlighting a noun phrase the way an it-cleft does, they foreground actions, needs, feelings, or the one point the speaker most wants to make.

The **what-cleft**: **What + clause + be + focused element**. The **all-cleft** works the same way but adds a limiting force - "this and only this" was the point.
"What he needs is more practice, not more advice."
"What surprised me most was how calm she stayed."
"All I wanted was a straight answer."

Two errors to know: never write "All **what** I wanted" - drop **what** entirely after **all**. And agreement follows the focused element: "What surprised me **was** how calm she was" (singular), not **were**. These structures sound deliberate, so use them where you actually want the emphasis - a plain sentence often reads more naturally.

data.summary: Use should you, were you to, and had you to form formal unreal or tentative conditionals without if.

examples.en: Should you require any assistance, let me know.

data.explanation:
English has three formal conditional patterns that drop **if** and use inversion instead. They carry the same conditional meaning, but the register shifts - common in professional correspondence, legal writing, and formal argument where plain **if** would feel too informal.

The three patterns: **Should + subject + base verb** (tentative future); **Were + subject + to + base verb** (unlikely or hypothetical); **Had + subject + past participle** (unreal past).
"Should you need further details, please contact us."
"Were she to accept, the team would start immediately."
"Had I known earlier, I'd have changed the plan."

Two errors to avoid: keeping **if** while also inverting ("If had I known" is wrong - pick one), and putting **will** or **would** inside the inverted clause. The conditional meaning is already carried by the inversion. Always use the base verb after **should**, and **to + base verb** after **were ... to**.

data.title: Subjunctive in Formal That-Clauses
data.summary: Use the subjunctive base form in formal that-clauses after verbs and adjectives of recommendation, necessity, or urgency.

examples.en: The doctor recommended that he reduce his working hours.
It is vital that every applicant bring photo ID.
She insisted that the figures be checked again.
We suggested that the launch wait until Monday.
It is important that the team respond quickly.
The committee demanded that the issue be reviewed.

data.explanation:
In formal English, certain verbs and adjectives of recommendation or necessity are followed by a **that-clause** where the verb holds its **base form** - regardless of the subject. This is the formal subjunctive. Standard in academic writing, professional reports, and official language.

Common **verb triggers**: recommend, suggest, insist, propose, demand, request. Common **adjective triggers**: essential, vital, important, necessary.
"The committee recommended that she **apply** again."
"It is vital that every participant **register** in advance."
"They insisted that the report **be** revised before publication."

The passive version uses **be** rather than **is** or **was** - "insisted that the draft **be** checked" - which often surprises learners. In everyday speech, **should + base verb** is an acceptable alternative, but the bare subjunctive is the formal choice. The single most common error: adding **-s** back ("It is essential that he **arrives**" - wrong; use **arrive**).

data.summary: Use advanced modal combinations to express nuanced certainty, likelihood, necessity, and future obligation.

examples.en: This may well be the last chance we get this year.

Advanced modal use is less about which modal to pick and more about combining modals with adverbs and auxiliary structures to hit a precise level of certainty or obligation. The differences between "might be", "may well be", and "might just be" are small in form but real in meaning.

**May well** sits closer to probability than possibility - the speaker considers something fairly likely.
"This may well be the best option we have."
**Might just** signals something barely within reach - narrow but real.
"We might just finish before the deadline if we start now."
**Would have to** introduces hypothetical necessity; **will have to** is unavoidable future obligation.
"If the funding falls through, we'd have to scale back."

Don't stack incompatible modals: "I might just can do it" is ungrammatical. One modal combination per clause. Also, **may well** never takes **to**: "it may well be true", not "it may well **to** be true". These forms work best in analytical or professional contexts where precision matters.

data.title: Discourse Markers in Formal English
data.summary: Use formal discourse markers to organise argument, contrast viewpoints, and guide the listener or reader through complex reasoning.

examples.en: The software is cheaper; moreover, it integrates well with our existing tools.
The road was crowded. Nonetheless, we arrived on time.
The data were incomplete; consequently, the review was postponed.
Our first option is faster. On the other hand, the second is less risky.
The northern route is scenic; in contrast, the motorway is efficient but dull.
Furthermore, the team has already tested a prototype.

data.explanation:
Formal **discourse markers** don't just connect sentences - they signal the logical relationship the reader should expect next. Choosing the wrong one creates a gap between what you signal and what you mean. At C1 level, that gap is noticed.

**Moreover** and **furthermore** add a supporting point. **Nonetheless** concedes a difficulty but holds a position. **Consequently** marks a direct result. **On the other hand** introduces a genuine alternative. **In contrast** marks a clear difference between two things.
"The software is cheaper; moreover, it integrates well with our current setup."
"The data were incomplete; consequently, the review was postponed."
"The northern route is faster. The southern, in contrast, avoids the toll roads."

Two persistent problems: using a formal marker where a simpler connector ("and", "but", "so") would sound more natural, and misreading the logical relationship. **Consequently** signals result - don't use it where you mean contrast. Position matters too: most of these markers belong at the start of a clause or after a semicolon, not mid-sentence.

data.explanation:
**Hedging** doesn't weaken writing - it makes it more precise. When a claim has limits, hedging signals that the speaker is aware of them. At C1 and above, knowing when and how to hedge is a mark of intellectual honesty, not vagueness.

Common hedging tools: **seems**, **appears**, **tends to**, **perhaps**, **somewhat**, **relatively**, **apparently**, and impersonal frames like **It would appear that** or **It seems that**.
"It seems that the original figures were entered twice."
"This method tends to work better with smaller groups."
"The opening section is somewhat unclear and may need revision."

The third example delivers a clear critique far more tactfully than "the opening section is bad" - same message, very different social effect. The risk is stacking too many hedges until the sentence says nothing: "Apparently it seems that the figures may perhaps be incorrect" is overloaded. Pick one or two hedges per sentence. **Emphatic do** and **fronting** give advanced speakers precise control over what a sentence stresses. Neither changes the facts - both change where the emphasis falls and how deliberately the sentence reads.

**Emphatic do/does/did** strengthens an affirmative statement. Always followed by the **base verb**.

**Fronting** moves a non-subject element to the start of the clause for rhetorical weight.

data.summary: Use ellipsis and substitution to avoid repetition and make speech and writing more natural and efficient.

**Ellipsis** and **substitution** are what make fluent English feel light. Instead of repeating words already established in context, speakers omit them or swap them for a stand-in. The result is more cohesive, less laboured prose or speech.

Ellipsis omits recoverable words entirely. Substitution replaces them: **one/ones** for countable nouns, **so/not** for clauses after think, hope, say, expect; auxiliary patterns for repeated predicates.
"She said she'd help, and she did."

The key is matching the substitute to what it replaces. **One** replaces a singular countable noun; **so** replaces a full clause - don't swap them. Only omit what the listener can genuinely recover from context. When in doubt, substitute rather than omit.

data.explanation:
**Reporting passives** let you present information without naming a source. The claim is foregrounded; the source is backgrounded. Standard in journalism, academic writing, and official communication when attribution is unknown, unimportant, or deliberately kept out of view.

Two patterns: **It + be + past participle + that-clause** (impersonal) and **subject + be + past participle + to-infinitive** (subject-focused).
"It is believed that the market will recover."
"The market is believed to be recovering."
"She is known to speak three languages." (stable fact - simple infinitive)
"The building is thought to have been damaged." (earlier event - perfect passive infinitive)

The infinitive choice after the subject-focused version carries real meaning: **to speak** (current or habitual), **to have been damaged** (completed passive event before the reporting moment). Mixing the two patterns is the main error: "It is said him to be difficult" and "The minister is said that he will resign" are both wrong - pick one pattern and follow it through.

examples.en: He denied changing the deadline without approval.

data.explanation:
At C1 level, **reported speech** is less about mechanical backshift and more about choosing the right **reporting verb** for the exact speech act. Each verb carries its own meaning and takes a specific grammatical pattern - getting both right is what gives professional writing its precision.

Key verb-pattern pairs:
**deny + ing**: "He denied changing the deadline."
**accuse + object + of + ing**: "She accused him of hiding the data."
**insist + formal that-clause**: "They insisted that the schedule remain unchanged."
**claim + perfect to-infinitive**: "The company claimed to have sent the warning."

The most common mistake is transferring one verb's pattern to another. "She suggested me to leave" is wrong - **suggest** doesn't take object + infinitive. "She accused that he lied" is wrong - **accuse** needs **object + of + ing**. The pattern is as fixed as the verb. Learn them as pairs, not separately.

data.title: Participle Clauses: Perfect and Passive
data.summary: Use perfect and passive participle clauses to show earlier time, cause, and compressed background information.

examples.en: Having reviewed the draft, I could see exactly where the problem was.
Having been warned about the traffic, we left before dawn.
Having finished lunch, they returned to the workshop.
Having been overlooked for years, the archive is finally being digitised.
Having studied the contract in detail, she noticed three inconsistencies.
Having been invited at short notice, I had little time to prepare.
Having missed the turn, we had to drive another ten miles.

whenToUse: Use: earlier completed action -> Having checked the figures, she sent the report.
Use: earlier passive condition -> Having been delayed twice, the launch felt risky.

data.explanation:
**Perfect participle clauses** compress a time relationship into a phrase - they signal that one action was completed before another, without needing a full subordinate clause. **Passive participle clauses** add the dimension of who performed the earlier action.

**Having + past participle**: the subject did something earlier.
"Having reviewed the draft, she sent her comments."
**Having been + past participle**: something was done to the subject earlier.
"Having been warned twice, he decided to stop."
"Having been delayed by bad weather, the team arrived late."

These clauses are common in formal writing and narrative prose - compact and deliberate. The critical rule: the implied subject of the participle clause must match the grammatical subject of the main clause. "Having checked the figures, the mistake became obvious" - wrong; the mistake didn't check anything. Fix: "Having checked the figures, I noticed the mistake." A dangling participle here isn't just awkward - it shifts the meaning.

data.summary: Use whose, of which, and preposition + relative pronoun patterns for more precise and formal reference.

examples.en: The company, whose profits fell sharply, announced a restructuring plan.

The committee, several members of which opposed the change, delayed the vote.

data.explanation:
At C1 level, the relative clause system extends well beyond **who**, **which**, and **that**. Formal writing regularly uses **whose** for possession, **preposition + which/whom** for precise relational meaning, and **of which** patterns for partitive or quantified reference.

**Whose** expresses possession for people, organisations, and sometimes things.
"The company, whose profits fell sharply, announced a restructuring."
**Preposition + which/whom** moves the preposition to the front - the formal alternative to stranding it at the end.
"The proposal to which everyone referred was never published."
"The researcher with whom I worked has since retired."
"The archive, much of which remains uncatalogued, is difficult to access."

Two reliable errors: writing "the company **which** profits fell" (needs **whose**), and using **that** after a preposition ("the proposal to **that** everyone objected" is wrong - use **which**). When a narrative is set in the past, any reference to what was going to happen **from that earlier viewpoint** uses past-oriented future forms. The three main tools each carry a different shade of meaning.

**Would** expresses expectation or inevitability from a past point.
"She knew the conversation would be difficult."

data.summary: Use advanced verb patterns such as verb + object + infinitive and verb + object + ing where needed.

examples.en: The coach encouraged the team to stay calm under pressure.
She reminded me to attach the final file.
The bad weather prevented us from leaving on time.

data.explanation:
A significant cluster of C1 verbs require an **object** between the main verb and the following verb form - and that object changes the shape of what comes next. The first verb controls the whole structure.

**Object + to-infinitive**: allow, encourage, persuade, remind, force, expect.
"They allowed us to leave early."
"She persuaded me to apply."
**Object + from + ing**: prevent, stop.
"The noise prevented him from sleeping."
**Object + ing**: catch, find (for observed action).
"I caught him reading my notes."

Meaning alone won't tell you the pattern. **Suggest** and **advise** seem similar, but "She suggested me to leave" is wrong; "She advised me to leave" is fine. **Remind** always needs an object before the infinitive: "he reminded **me** to send the report", not "he reminded to send the report". The fix: learn each verb with its complement as a single fixed unit, not separately.

data.title: Determiners and Quantifiers: No, Not Any, Any, Every, Scarcely Any
data.summary: Use these forms more precisely to express absence, free choice, universality, and very limited quantity.

examples.en: There was no reason to delay the decision.
We couldnt find any reliable evidence.
examples.note: absence with not any meaning through verb negative

examples.en: You can choose any seat in the back row.
Every detail in the contract matters here.
There was scarcely any traffic at dawn.
Scarcely any students had finished before lunch.
No one on the team objected to the change.
I dont have any strong preference either way.

whenToUse: Use: direct absence -> There was no warning at all.
Use: softer absence -> We didn't see any obvious damage.
Use: free choice -> You can ask any member of staff.
Use: universal coverage -> Every applicant must sign here.
Use: very limited amount -> There was scarcely any light in the corridor.
data.explanation:
At C1 level, determiner choices do more than express quantity - they signal scope, tone, and logical type. **No** and **not any** both express absence, but **no** is more direct and carries more finality; **not any** distributes the negation through the verb.
"There was no warning." vs. "We didn't receive any warning."

**Any** in affirmative contexts expresses **free choice** - whichever item you select - rather than negation.
"You can ask any member of staff." (= whichever one you choose)
**Every** distributes universally, treating each item individually rather than as a group: "Every detail in the contract matters."
**Scarcely any** expresses an extremely limited quantity - closer to "almost none" than "a little" - and fits formal or written registers.
"There was scarcely any light in the corridor."

Agreement traps: **every** always takes a **singular noun** (every student, not every students). **Scarcely any people** takes **plural agreement** because **people** is plural - don't let the negative feel of **scarcely** push you toward singular.

data.title: Articles: Idiomatic and Zero-Article Patterns
data.summary: Use articles accurately in idiomatic expressions and advanced zero-article patterns.

examples.en: He went to bed straight after the flight.
Shes still at work, so call later.
We travelled by train and returned by coach.
The children are on foot, so theyll arrive later.
He got into trouble for ignoring the safety rules.
My aunt spent years at sea when she was younger.
We had lunch at home and worked in the garden.
She was in charge of the whole event.

whenToUse: Use: daily routine idiom -> She's at work right now.
Use: transport -> We went by train but came back in the car.

Use: routine action -> I usually go to bed before midnight.
data.explanation:
Many high-frequency English expressions use **zero article**, and adding **the** where it doesn't belong is one of the most persistent C1 errors. These patterns are partly grammatical and partly idiomatic - there's no single rule that covers them all.

Fixed zero-article expressions: **at work, at home, go to bed, in trouble, at sea, in charge, by car, on foot, in hospital** (BrE for being admitted). Adding **the** changes the meaning or breaks the phrase entirely.
"He went to bed." (sleeping) vs. "He went to **the** bed." (a specific piece of furniture)
"She's at work." (working) vs. "She's at **the** office." (physically in the building)

Transport expressions split by method vs. specific vehicle: **by car** (how you travelled) vs. **in the car** (which specific car). Both can be correct depending on what you mean. The most practical approach: learn these expressions as **fixed chunks**. Once you know "go to bed, by train, in trouble, at sea", the article is already baked into the chunk - you don't need to reason through the rule each time.

data.title: Punctuation for Meaning
data.summary: Use commas, semicolons, and dashes to shape meaning, pace, and clarity in complex sentences.

examples.en: The proposal, which had already been revised twice, was still unclear.
The weather had improved; however, the roads were still unsafe.
We met in Paris, France; Porto, Portugal; and Ghent, Belgium.
He made one final point - and it changed the whole discussion.
Having reviewed the numbers, we postponed the launch.
The test was long, but fair.

examples.en: My supervisor, rather surprisingly, agreed immediately.
The report was complete; the budget, however, was not.

whenToUse: Use: non-defining information -> My manager, who joined last year, approved it.
Use: link closely related clauses -> The evidence was limited; the conclusion was cautious.
Use: clarify lists -> We invited Aylin, the designer; Reza, the developer; and Sara, the editor.
Use: add emphatic explanation -> There was only one option left - delay the launch.
data.explanation:
In writing, **punctuation is structure**. A comma, a semicolon, and a dash are not interchangeable pauses - each signals a different relationship between clauses, and using the wrong one changes meaning or readability.

**Commas** mark non-defining information, introductory elements, and coordinate clause boundaries.
"My supervisor, who joined last year, approved it." (commas signal extra, not defining, information - remove them and the meaning shifts)
**Semicolons** link closely related independent clauses, or separate complex list items that already contain commas.
"The evidence was thin; the conclusion was cautious."
**Dashes** introduce an emphatic explanation or afterthought with more force than a comma.
"He made one final point - and it changed the whole discussion."

Two persistent mistakes: the **comma splice** ("The figures were incomplete, therefore we delayed" - use a semicolon or period before **therefore**), and overusing dashes until every sentence feels urgent. Choose punctuation by the **relationship** you're signalling, not by how long a pause feels in your head.

data.title: Complex Sentence Linking with Subordination
data.summary: Use layered subordination to build precise complex sentences while keeping time, cause, concession, and condition relationships clear.

examples.en: Although the original timeline was too short, we continued because the client had already announced the date.
If the servers fail again when traffic peaks, the platform could become unstable.
The report, which was completed under pressure, still reads clearly because the structure is strong.
Since the team had already tested the backup, they were confident, even though the rollout remained risky.
When the final draft arrives, if the budget section is complete, Ill send it on immediately.
Because the samples were damaged before they reached the lab, the results had to be treated cautiously.
Although she agreed in principle, she asked for revisions before the proposal was shared.
If we want the message to be clear, we need to cut the details that distract from the main point.

whenToUse: Use: combine concession and cause -> Although the plan was risky, we accepted it because the alternative was worse.
Use: combine time and condition -> If the figures improve when the final data arrive, we'll revise the forecast.
Use: layer description -> The office, which had already been renovated, still felt cramped because the layout was poor.
Use: formal explanation -> Since the first option had failed, we chose the second, even though it was more expensive.
data.explanation:
**Complex sentences** work when every clause earns its place and the hierarchy is clear: one main claim, supported by subordinate clauses that each show a specific relationship - cause, concession, condition, time, or description. The skill at C1 level is knowing which linker creates which relationship, and how to layer them without losing the logic.

A well-built complex sentence handles multiple relationships at once.
"Although the timeline was tight, we agreed to continue because the client had already announced the date."
"Since the first approach had failed, we chose the second, even though it cost more."
The main clause carries the weight; subordinate clauses specify conditions, reasons, or qualifications.

The most common failure is competing linkers: "Although **because** the data were late..." - pick one relationship. The same applies to stacking **if** and **when** in the same clause when only one is doing real work. Long subordinate sentences also need commas to guide the reader through - without them, clause boundaries blur. Complexity should make meaning **sharper**, not harder to follow.
